question: According to data in the latest report by the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, the amount of VAT and customs duty fraud currently under investigation amounts to EUR 45.01 billion – representing 67 % of the estimated losses to the budgets of the EU and the Member States.

The findings point to the consolidation of criminal networks that have taken control of significant segments of the fraud chain, exploiting global supply chains, shadow banking systems, and operational structures that have been infiltrated in European ports and trade depots, with cross-cutting impacts on strategic sectors of the economy and links to other illicit activities, including drug and human trafficking.

This intensification of organised crime affecting the EU’s own revenue takes place at a particularly sensitive time, when the next multiannual financial framework (MFF) is being negotiated, with more flexibility provided for in the implementation of funds by Member States, which could amplify structural vulnerabilities to fraud, corruption and criminal infiltration.

Could the Commission provide a detailed response to the following: What strategic assessment does it make of the role these criminal networks are playing in reshaping the European criminal ecosystem, including the use of clandestine banking systems, front companies, bogus logistics networks, and tax-evasion and money-laundering structures, and what geopolitical aspects does it identify in this situation?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.5.2026) The Commission shares the concerns about organised value added tax (VAT) and customs duty fraud and their impact on Member States and, indirectly, the EU budget, economy and security. Europol’s 2025 Serious and Organised Crime Threat Assessment confirms1 that fraud remains a serious and persistent threat.

As announced in ProtectEU: a European Internal Security Strategy2, the Commission will propose to reinforce the mandates of Europol and Eurojust and modernise the rules to fight against organised crime in 2026.

In addition, the European Public Prosecutor’s Office investigates and prosecutes criminal offences affecting EU’s financial interests, while the European Anti-Fraud Office conducts administrative investigations into irregularities against the EU budget.

The Commission also supports the European Multidisciplinary Platform Against Criminal Threats operational action plan on VAT and Missing Trader IntraCommunity fraud3. The Commission is currently reviewing the EU’s Anti-Fraud Architecture, to strengthen the protection of the EU’s financial interests.

The aim is to modernise the EU’s anti-fraud framework and, thus, strengthen the EU’s capacity to detect and combat crimes affecting the EU budget, including VAT and customs fraud. To implement the follow-the-money approach, the Commission calls for swift transposition of the Directive on asset recovery and confiscation4.

Once operational, the new EU Customs Authority and EU Customs Data Hub5 will better equip customs to perform risk analysis and further improve cooperation between all law enforcement bodies. Together, these measures will better equip the EU and Member States to disrupt criminal networks and better protect Europe’s security, economy and financial system.
